Zillow key metrics — marketplace mix, take-rate, falsifiers (v5)

Z-pilot-2026-09-21-v5 · USD · series 2026-09-21T21:00:00Z · built 2026-09-22 02:48 UTC

The short version

Own Z for five to ten years. The business is a housing marketplace with data and network effects. The fear that agentic AI kills the consumer front door is the mispricing. What would change that view first is a sustained drop in monthly audience or audience share. A second warning would be Google or ChatGPT taking a meaningful and rising slice of housing search (roughly five percent or more). Local MLS color such as MRED / Chicagoland is ops detail, not a substitute for those KPIs.

As of: 2026-09-21 (ET)

Zillow is not a banner-ad shop waiting for ChatGPT to erase it. It is a housing marketplace. It owns a large share of how people look for homes and rentals, turns that attention into validated connections for agents and landlords, and is shifting more of those connections into products that pay for outcomes rather than noise.

A second engine — Rentals — and an attach product — Zillow Home Loans — ride the same front door. The stock still often prices as if that front door were fragile and as if GAAP earnings were the whole story. The metrics below are the scoreboard that decides whether that fear is earned.

1. What Zillow is and how it makes money

Zillow Group runs consumer brands — Zillow, Trulia, StreetEasy, HotPads — that pull demand for homes and apartments. Revenue shows up in three reportable engines:

1. Residential — Premier Agent and Preferred-style connection advertising, plus related for-sale marketplace products. 2. Mortgages — including Zillow Home Loans (ZHL), the company’s purchase-mortgage origination business. 3. Rentals — multifamily and rental marketplace revenue.

Starting with fourth-quarter 2024 results, the company prints a For Sale subtotal — Residential plus Mortgages, managed together. Rentals stands alone. Comparative filings and later letters now also backfill For Sale for earlier hole periods: full-year 2022 $1,641M, full-year 2023 $1,548M, fourth-quarter 2023 $371M, and the first three quarters of 2024 $424M / $443M / $444M. The only true silence left on the modern Residential and Mortgages spine is first through third quarter 2023 — those three chart points stay Residential plus Mortgages summed and marked derived ($387M / $404M / $386M). They are not written into the For Sale fact column. Do not treat Homes-era schemes as For Sale. Plot Residential and Mortgages on their own mix chart as themselves. Adjusted EBITDA is the non-GAAP operating pulse management highlights next to GAAP net income.

Fourth-quarter letter prints that lock the year-end segment picture:

By the second quarter of 2026 the company printed $772M total revenue, $549M For Sale, $209M Rentals, Adjusted EBITDA $176M, and a slight GAAP loss (−$4M). Cash and investments were $572M. Survival is not the open question. Mix quality and take-rate are.

Revenue, adjusted EBITDA, and GAAP net income sit side by side. They are never stacked. Total revenue and GAAP net income run as far as the clean prints go, and the chart keeps the shorter of ten years and that span. Adjusted EBITDA on the same chart stays on the recent window, because earlier cells are not scale-safe. GAAP net income is the honesty check next to the non-GAAP operating pulse.

2. Growth engine vs legacy core

Think of the stack as two stories sharing one front door.

Legacy core — the For Sale marketplace. Still the largest dollar engine (full-year 2025 For Sale $1,903M; full-year 2023 For Sale $1,548M; full-year 2022 For Sale $1,641M). Inside it, monetization is migrating from share-of-voice and legacy ads toward Preferred (a success-fee style product) and Enhanced-market connection mix. That migration is the growth story inside the core — not a separate segment line on the income statement.

Growth engines — Rentals and ZHL attach. Rentals is the clear second locomotive: Q2’26 $209M versus Q2’25 $159M. ZHL purchase origination is the attach flywheel on the same buyers: Q2’26 $2.174B versus Q2’25 $1.116B. The fourth-quarter letter prints alone run $487M → $923M → $1.5B across Q4’23 through Q4’25.

The front door that feeds both engines is still enormous. Using Comscore figures the company itself quotes (not a licensed Comscore feed), Zillow Group held about 70% of the real-estate audience in both first-quarter and second-quarter 2026. That is the network-and-attention moat print — and also the first place a falsifier would show up.

3. Walk the lines — growth, decline, proving KPIs

3a. Audience — soft, not collapsing

Quarterly visits and average monthly unique users (AMUU):

  • Q2’26: visits 2,529M / AMUU 239M, versus Q2’25 2,590M / 243M
  • Q1’26: 2,276M / 220M, versus Q1’25 2,354M / 227M
  • Locked AMUU fills the issuer did print: Q1’24 217, Q2’24 231

That is seasonal noise and a soft year-over-year comparison — not a sustained audience collapse. Do not drop full-year visit totals (for example full-year 2025 9,593M) onto the quarterly chart. The traffic chart keeps the shorter of ten years and the quarters that have numbers.

The visits and AMUU chart is side by side only — the two metrics are not additive.

Audience share near 70% on those issuer-quoted Comscore prints is a sharper falsifier lens than raw AMUU. Google or ChatGPT housing-search share is still a gap in the cabinet — a watch item, not a live series.

3b. For Sale core — take-rate slope and Preferred mix

Primary proving KPI — For Sale revenue as basis points of industry total transaction value, trailing twelve months:

10.1 (full-year 2024) → 10.2 / 10.3 / 10.1 (first through third quarter 2025) → 8.5 (full-year 2025) → 8.7 (first-quarter 2026) → 8.8 (second-quarter 2026).

The step from roughly ten basis points in mid-2025 into the high-8s is the live monetization slope. The National Association of Realtors total-transaction-value methodology shift begins in the fourth-quarter 2025 window — the slope and the method change overlap, so the chart carries that banner.

Attachment mix — Preferred or Enhanced share of connections (this is mix of connections, not share of revenue):

21% → 24 → 27 → 34 → 44 → 49% from year-end 2024 through first-quarter 2026. Company guide: more than 75% of connections in Preferred by year-end 2026.

A separate print, not a seventh point on that line: in second-quarter 2026 the letter said 61% of connections were on the integrated experience through Preferred partners.

The standalone Preferred / Enhanced percentage for second-quarter 2026 itself was not printed.

Relative unit-econ proof (not a dollar figure per connection): Preferred generated +23% revenue per connection versus legacy in 2025; outlook +35% by end-2026. Absolute connection count and a clean dollars-per-connection figure remain a gap.

Anti-pattern: For Sale dollars times Enhanced percentage is not Preferred revenue. Enhanced percentage is connection mix, not revenue share.

3c. Rentals — the compounding second engine

Rentals revenue: Q4’23 $93M → Q4’24 $116M → Q4’25 $168M; Q2’26 $209M versus Q2’25 $159M. This is the cleanest growth line on the scoreboard — same front door, different landlord wallet.

3d. Mortgages / ZHL — attach, not a trading desk

Mortgages revenue is still small next to Residential (Q2’26 Mortgages $84M versus Residential $465M), but the volume KPI that proves attach is ZHL purchase origination: letter-locked fourth quarters $487M / $923M / $1.5B, and Q2’26 $2.174B. Do not back into a fourth-quarter figure by subtracting earlier quarters from the annual total when a letter print exists. Refinance and total (purchase plus refinance) origination dollars for those fourth quarters remain a gap.

4. Unit economics → valuation

Valuation for this pack follows the desk hierarchy, not a made-up revenue per connection:

1. For Sale / TTV trailing basis points — take intensity without inventing connection count. 2. Preferred / Enhanced attachment percentage — leading indicator for mix into richer connections. 3. +23% / +35% revenue-per-connection uplift — relative pricing and conversion quality. 4. Dollars per connection — only under an explicit connection count (a gap today).

Shape math (derived, not dollars): at attachment rate \(m\) and uplift \(R\), Preferred’s share of connection revenue is \(m(1+R)/(1+mR)\). At m=49% and R=23% that is roughly 54% of connection revenue; at m=75% and R=35% roughly 80%. That is why mix understates Preferred’s economic weight — and it still does not unlock For Sale times m as Preferred revenue.
